name: Abū ʿAlī al-Ḥasan ibn Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd al-Ghaffār al-Fārisī al-Fasawī
summary: The great grammarian of the Buyid courts, author of al-Īḍāḥ and al-Takmila for ʿAḍud al-Dawla, and the teacher of Ibn Jinnī.
bio: Abū ʿAlī was born in Fasā in Fārs in 288/900 and came to Baghdad young, where he learnt from al-Zajjāj, Ibn al-Sarrāj and al-Akhfash al-Aṣghar. Al-Zubaydī, writing in his lifetime, puts him in the tenth Basran generation and sums up his career in a line: he was with Ibn Ḥamdān (Sayf al-Dawla, in Aleppo), the Daylamite ruler called him to teach his nephews, he stayed in Baghdad, then went to Shiraz.

In Shiraz he taught the Buyid ʿAḍud al-Dawla and wrote for him al-Īḍāḥ, on syntax, and al-Takmila, on morphology. The biographers tell that the ruler found al-Īḍāḥ too slight, 'fit for boys', and that al-Fārisī answered with al-Takmila. His collections of questions, named after the cities where they were asked (al-Baghdādiyyāt, al-Ḥalabiyyāt, al-Shīrāziyyāt, al-ʿAskariyyāt), and his al-Ḥujja on the causes of the seven Qurʾān readings show him at his best, a master of qiyās.

His meeting with Ibn Jinnī is one of the best-known stories of the grammarians. As Yāqūt tells it, he passed through the mosque of Mosul and found a young man teaching, explaining how wāw turns to alif in qāla and qāma; he put an objection the young man could not answer and said, 'You have turned to raisin while still a sour grape' (tazabbabta wa-anta ḥiṣrim). Ibn Jinnī asked who he was, left his circle and followed him for the rest of his teacher's life, some forty years. Ibn Khallikān tells it otherwise: Ibn Jinnī had studied with him before and set up on his own too soon. Al-Fārisī died in Baghdad in 377/987.
uncertain: Al-Zubaydī and the TDV count him a Basran; later histories of the schools count him among the Baghdadis who joined Basra and Kufa.
